analysis.one_liner: Sets national patient protections for managed-care health plans, including outside appeals when care is denied.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final three weeks of the 106th Congress by Sen. Kennedy with one cosponsor, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of enforceable patient protections into federal law for people in managed-care and employer health plans. It required plans to review care denials quickly, let patients appeal denials to independent outside reviewers whose decisions bind the plan, guaranteed direct access to OB-GYNs, pediatricians, and emergency care, barred contracts that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options, and opened the door to lawsuits against plans by limiting a federal law (ERISA) that currently shields employer plans from most patient lawsuits. It also required plans to disclose plain-language information about benefits, costs, and appeal rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in managed-care plans and employer-sponsored health coverage. Someone whose plan denies a treatment could appeal internally within strict deadlines and then to an independent outside panel at a filing fee of at most $25 — waived for people with low incomes and refunded if the appeal succeeds. Patients get direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care without a referral, emergency care covered under a 'prudent layperson' standard without prior approval, standing referrals to specialists for chronic conditions, continued treatment from a doctor whose contract ends mid-treatment (through pregnancy, terminal illness, or scheduled surgery), coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, and disclosure of what their plan covers and how doctors are paid. Contracts that gag doctors from discussing treatment are void.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in managed-care and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to decide prior-authorization requests within 14 days (72 hours in urgent cases) and treats a missed deadline as a denial patients can appeal, and establishes internal and independent external appeals for denials based on medical judgment [S2][S3].

Guarantees access to emergency services without prior authorization and without extra cost even at out-of-network hospitals, direct access to obstetrical, gynecological, and pediatric care, standing referrals to specialists, and continuation of care when a provider's contract ends mid-treatment [S2][S3].

Covers routine patient costs for people with life-threatening or serious illnesses joining federally approved clinical trials, and requires plans to pay claims promptly and disclose benefit, cost, and appeals information in understandable form [S2][S3].

Bars plans from paying reviewers in ways that encourage claim denials, voids contract clauses restricting doctors' medical communications with patients, makes outside appeal decisions binding on plans, and imposes penalties up to $1,000 a day on officials who refuse to carry out an approved appeal [S3].
Limits the ERISA preemption that currently blocks many lawsuits over denied health coverage, and preserves patients' existing state-law and federal rights to sue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed-care plans bear the compliance costs: faster review deadlines, outside appeal processes, binding reversal of denials, claim-payment deadlines, and disclosure requirements. Employers sponsoring self-insured plans face the same standards and, because the bill narrows ERISA preemption, potential lawsuits over denied care. Some of these costs would flow into premiums; enrollees choosing the new point-of-service option pay its extra premium and cost-sharing themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, managed-care plans, and employers

drawbacks.text: Plans and insurers face real compliance costs — expedited timelines, external review contracts, penalties for missed deadlines — that would likely be passed into premiums, and the non-network coverage option's added premium and cost-sharing are borne by the enrollee who chooses it [S3].

Narrowing ERISA preemption (Sec. 302) would expose employer health plans to litigation over coverage decisions, a cost employers and business groups warned would drive up coverage costs, though the bill includes limitations on actions and preserves plan protections [S3].

A patient appealing a denial externally may have to pay a filing fee of up to $25 unless certified as indigent, and external review excludes disputes about plan exclusions or eligibility that do not involve medical judgment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are substantial and specific — enforceable appeal rights with deadlines, binding outside review, and direct access to OB-GYN, pediatric, and emergency care address real, well-documented harms of 1990s managed care. The costs are genuine: faster decisions, independent appeals, and expanded litigation exposure would raise administrative and legal expenses, some portion of which reaches premiums. The bill tried to limit this (appeal costs fall on plans, fees are small and refundable, lawsuits face limitations), so the design is reasonable for what it attempts; the honest objection is about magnitude of cost, not its existence.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with only weeks left in the session, it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, where it sat until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 — no committee action, no debate, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Kennedy introduced S. 3057 on September 15, 2000, and it was read a first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar [S1][S5].
On September 18, 2000, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 808) [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill never received a Senate vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed-care plans, which avoided the compliance costs, binding outside appeals, and expanded litigation exposure the bill would have imposed. Patients who would have gained enforceable appeal rights and direct access to specialists lost the chance for those protections in that Congress.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor listed.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever recorded, so the chamber's split cannot be measured from this record; the bill died on the calendar with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill binds them to strict claim and appeal deadlines, independent external reviews whose reversals are binding, bans on incentives that reward denial of claims, and disclosure of benefit and compensation practices. These are costs paid for by faster, more patient-favorable coverage decisions for the public.

Employer plans governed by ERISA would face the same patient-protection standards and, because Sec. 302 limits ERISA preemption, could be sued over denied care — a cost many would pass into employee premiums, in exchange for enforceable appeal rights for their workers.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys and health care providers
industries.note: Narrowing ERISA preemption and adding penalties for refusing approved benefits creates grounds for legal action over denied care, and doctors gain protection from contract gag clauses and continued payment when contracts end mid-treatment.
